passage: The HR room at the agency smelled of coffee and toner. Payal placed her resignation letter on the desk. “Three months' notice, and I've written a handover plan for every client,” she said. Nilesh, the HR manager, glanced at it. “Is there anything that would make you stay?” Payal breathed out. “I have thought about it for weeks. I asked my head twice for changes in how juniors are spoken to and how numbers are reported. Nothing shifted, and I can't live inside that any more.” Through the glass, two people from her team pretended to sort files. The team head walked past without turning. “I'd like to leave properly,” Payal said. Nilesh nodded and slid a pen across.

qa.q: How much notice did Payal offer?
qa.a: Payal offered three months' notice.

qa.q: What is Payal feeling when Payal says, “I can't live inside that any more”?
qa.a: Payal is settled but weary after weeks of thought: the workplace's ways are ones that Payal cannot accept, and the calm handover plan shows a wish to leave with dignity.

qa.q: What made Payal's exit calm and not a blow-up?
qa.a: Payal asked for changes twice first, wrote a handover plan for every client and gave three months' notice, so the departure was planned, not angry.

qa.q: How might the two people from Payal's team have felt as they watched through the glass?
qa.a: They may have felt unsettled, torn between curiosity and worry about their own place, which fits pretending to sort files instead of looking away.

grounding: An employee who cannot live with a workplace's values weighs options and plans a calm exit with dignity.

passage:
Subject: Decision
Dear Jyoti,
Thank you for the coffee last Sunday. You asked whether I was sure, so here is my honest reasoning. For eight months I have watched the team praise whoever shouts loudest and quietly blame whoever isn't in the room. At first I told myself to adapt. Last week I caught myself rehearsing the same lines, and I didn't like the sound of them. I have listed what I can control: I'll finish the current project properly, give clear notice in April, update my portfolio and speak to two people in the industry whom I trust. I'll also thank the colleagues who were kind. Staying and shrinking would cost me more slowly than leaving. I would like to leave with my name intact.
Pankaj

qa.q: In which month does Pankaj plan to give notice?
qa.a: Pankaj plans to give clear notice in April.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj say, “I didn't like the sound of them”?
qa.a: Pankaj was alarmed to hear the workplace's habits in Pankaj's own voice, which suggests shrinking to fit had already started.

qa.q: What steps has Pankaj listed to leave well?
qa.a: Pankaj will finish the project, give clear notice in April, update the portfolio, speak to two trusted people in the industry and thank the kind colleagues.

qa.q: How might Jyoti take this email after asking whether Pankaj was sure?
qa.a: Jyoti may feel reassured that the decision is careful and not rushed, since the email lays out reasons and a plan.

grounding: An employee who finds a workplace's values impossible to live with weighs options and plans a calm exit.

passage: Sabina, you asked why I finally quit the firm. This is Alka's honest answer, over this terrible coffee. It wasn't one big thing. It was the manager telling us to write 'minor delay' when a client's shipment was stuck for three weeks. It was the way people laughed at the cleaner's accent in the pantry, and I laughed too, once, and hated myself on the metro home. I noticed I'd stopped saying what I thought in meetings. I was getting smaller. So I made a plan. I spent two months applying quietly, finished my projects properly and wrote a clear handover. On my last day I thanked my team, shook my manager's hand and left. No drama. I just didn't want to become someone I'd avoid.

qa.q: What did the manager tell them to write when the shipment was stuck?
qa.a: 'Minor delay'.

qa.q: How did Alka feel after laughing at the cleaner's accent?
qa.a: Alka felt ashamed and disgusted with Alka's own behaviour on the metro home.

qa.q: What made Alka's exit dignified?
qa.a: Planning calmly: applying quietly for two months, finishing projects, writing a clear handover and thanking the team without drama.

qa.q: How might Alka's team feel about the calm goodbye?
qa.a: They were left with a proper handover and thanks, so they likely respected the exit, even if some wondered why Alka left.

grounding: An employee who can no longer live with a workplace's values plans a calm, dignified exit rather than shrinking.

passage: I sat next to Ankita for two years at the insurance call centre, so I saw most of it. When Jatin, our team manager, began telling us to 'forget' to mention the cancellation option to customers, Ankita went very quiet. She stopped joining the evening chai round. Twice I saw her step outside after a call and just stand by the parking lot. She never argued with Jatin in front of us. But she started coming in early with a notebook, and one day I saw an interview confirmation on her phone. Three weeks later she handed Jatin a letter, finished every pending ticket and trained the new girl for two full days. On her last evening she hugged me and said, 'I couldn't keep saying those lines.' I still wonder if I should have left too.

qa.q: What did Jatin tell the team to 'forget' to mention?
qa.a: The cancellation option to customers.

qa.q: What might Ankita have been feeling when she stood by the parking lot after calls?
qa.a: She seemed troubled and uneasy, unable to live with saying those lines, even though she never argued openly.

qa.q: What made Ankita's exit calm and dignified?
qa.a: She planned quietly, handed in a letter, finished every pending ticket and trained the new colleague for two full days.

qa.q: How might the new girl experience Ankita's last weeks?
qa.a: She got two full days of careful training, so she probably felt supported, perhaps without knowing why Ankita was leaving.

grounding: A colleague's account of an employee who could not accept a workplace's values and planned a calm exit.

passage: January: at the tour company in Gangtok, Kiran watched the owner overcharge a group of students and joke about it at dinner. Everyone laughed. Kiran didn't, and lay awake that night. February: it happened twice more, and Kiran felt like someone who had learned to say nothing. Over momos, Kiran told Pema, a friend from college, 'I don't recognise myself at work.' Pema asked, 'What would leaving with your head up look like?' They wrote a list: a few months of savings, two other agencies, a date. March, a clear Monday: Kiran gave a month's notice, finished the spring bookings and left a neat file for whoever came next. On the last bus down the hill, Kiran felt scared and oddly light.

qa.q: What did the owner joke about at dinner in January?
qa.a: Overcharging a group of students.

qa.q: What did Kiran mean by 'I don't recognise myself at work'?
qa.a: Kiran felt uneasy and ashamed about staying silent, as if slowly shrinking into someone else.

qa.q: How did Pema's question help?
qa.a: 'What would leaving with your head up look like?' turned the distress into a plan: savings, other agencies and a date.

qa.q: How might whoever replaces Kiran benefit from the way Kiran left?
qa.a: They inherit finished spring bookings and a neat file, so they can start smoothly.

grounding: Over three months an employee decides a workplace's values are unliveable and plans a calm, dignified exit.

passage: You're asking if leaving means failing, Salma? Let your Sharmila Khala tell you something. At twenty-five I worked at a big export house in Tiruppur. Good job, and a boss who made us sign quality papers for batches we had never checked. Everyone signed. My friend Revathi said, "Close your eyes, it's how things are done." For months I shrank. I stopped laughing at lunch. I stopped telling my mother anything about work. One night I sat with a notebook and wrote two columns: what staying was costing me, and what leaving would cost. The first column was longer. I didn't storm out. I found another job, finished my pending orders, trained the girl who replaced me, and left with a proper letter. Revathi didn't speak to me for a month. Two years later, she left too.

qa.q: What were the workers made to sign?
qa.a: They signed quality papers for batches they had never checked.

qa.q: What does young Sharmila's shrinking show she was feeling?
qa.a: She was unhappy and uneasy, slowly losing herself; she stopped laughing at lunch and stopped telling her mother about work.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why was her way of leaving wise?
qa.a: Writing the two columns showed that staying cost more; she then found another job and finished her work first, so she left with dignity.

qa.q: Why might Revathi have stopped speaking to Sharmila for a month?
qa.a: Revathi may have felt judged or left behind, since the leaving questioned the habit Revathi had accepted.

grounding: Sharmila Khala recalls weighing a workplace whose values she could not live with and planning a calm, dignified exit.
